title: How To Handle Parent Complaints About Grades
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin lays out a four-step method for handling parent complaints about grades without either angering the parent or compromising grading integrity. Step one is to speak directly by phone or in person rather than by email, since tone is easily misread in writing. Step two is to listen fully before responding, letting the parent feel heard. Step three, 'give the why,' requires the teacher to justify the grade with an objective measure — a score, percentage, or rubric — rather than a vague impression. Step four is to provide the student a concrete way forward, shifting responsibility for improvement back onto the student rather than the teacher. Linsin emphasizes that a calm, friendly demeanor during the conversation is the single biggest factor in whether the meeting succeeds, since defensiveness can escalate a complaint into one made to the principal.
points: Handle grade complaints by phone or in person, not email, so you control tone rather than risk being misread.
Listen fully and let the parent voice their frustration before you respond.
Justify every grade with an objective measure — a percentage, score, or rubric — never a vague impression.
Give the parent a concrete next step the student can take to improve the grade, shifting responsibility to the student.
A calm, friendly demeanor is the single most important factor in a successful grade-complaint meeting.
quotes: Thus, it’s best to speak directly to the parent—if not in person, then over the phone. This way, you control the tone and spirit of your message, which is even more important than what you actually say.
Your first order of business is to just listen and grasp the crux of their complaint . You must get to the bottom of why they’re unhappy. Often, it’s different than you expect.
You must be able to share a percentage, score, unmet standard, rubric, inventory, key, or other objective measure. Always, always, always.
With the parent’s understanding of the grade, and what it takes to improve it, you’ll empower them to help and support their child. They’ll also leave the meeting with a greater appreciation of you.
It’s important to emphasize that a calm and friendly demeanor is the number one key to a successful meeting with parents. Any defensiveness or hostility from you will sabotage the process.
